content: Letermovir is indicated for the prevention of cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection and disease in adult CMV-seropositive recipients ([R+]) of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplants (HSCT). The recommended dosage is 480 mg orally or intravenously once daily. This can be administered as one 480 mg tablet, two 240 mg tablets, or four 120 mg oral pellet packets for patients unable to swallow tablets. Prophylaxis should begin between Day 0 and Day 28 post-transplantation (before or after engraftment) and continue through Day 100. For patients at risk of late CMV infection, prophylaxis may be extended through Day 200 post-HSCT. Letermovir is also indicated for the prevention of CMV disease in adult kidney transplant recipients at high risk (donor CMV-seropositive/recipient CMV-seronegative [D+/R-]). The dosage is the same as for HSCT recipients, with prophylaxis initiated between Day 0 and Day 7 post-transplant and continued through Day 200. Following completion of prophylaxis, monitoring for CMV reactivation is recommended. Intravenous administration should only be used in patients unable to take oral therapy, and a switch to oral administration should occur as soon as feasible. The tablet and injection formulations are interchangeable without dosage adjustment, as determined by the physician. No dosage adjustment is required based on age. However, letermovir significantly interacts with other drugs due to its effects on hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with certain drugs is contraindicated due to the risk of severe adverse effects or toxicity. 1. Ergot Alkaloids (e.g., dihydroergotamine, ergotamine): Letermovir increases their levels, leading to a risk of ergotism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 2. Lonafarnib: Letermovir increases its levels, and co-administration is contraindicated due to its sensitivity to CYP3A4 inhibition. 3. Pimozide: Letermovir increases pimozide levels, posing a risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Co-administration is contraindicated. 4. Pitavastatin and Simvastatin: Letermovir increases their levels, especially when co-administered with cyclosporine, leading to a risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis. Co-administration is contraindicated. 5. Apalutamide: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 6. Avapritinib: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided, or the avapritinib dose should be reduced if unavoidable. 7. Carbamazepine: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 8. Ceftobiprole: Letermovir levels may increase due to OATP1B1/1B3 inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 9. Efavirenz: This drug decreases letermovir levels via UGT1A1/3 induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 10. Elacestrant: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. 11. Enasidenib: Letermovir levels may increase due to OATP1B1/1B3 or BCRP inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 12. Encorafenib: Letermovir increases its levels. If co-administration is unavoidable, the encorafenib dose should be halved. 13. Entrectinib: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. 14. Fosphenytoin: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 15. Infigratinib: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. 16. Lasmiditan: This drug increases letermovir levels via P-gp inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 17. Lemborexant: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration with moderate or strong CYP3A inhibitors is not recommended. 18. Leniolisib: Letermovir levels may increase due to OATP1B1/1B3 inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 19. Lurbinectedin: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. 20. Midazolam (intranasal): Letermovir increases its levels, potentially prolonging sedation. Co-administration should be avoided. 21. Nefazodone: This drug increases letermovir levels via P-gp inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 22. Nirogacestat: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. 23. Omaveloxolone: Letermovir increases its levels. If unavoidable, reduce the omaveloxolone dose to 100 mg/day and monitor for adverse effects. 24. Oxcarbazepine: This drug decreases letermovir levels via UGT1A1/3 induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 25. Pacritinib: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration should be avoided. 26. Pemigatinib: Letermovir increases its levels. If co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the pemigatinib dose. 27. Pexidartinib: Letermovir increases its levels. If co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the pexidartinib dose. 28. Phenobarbital: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 29. Phenytoin: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 30. Primidone: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 31. Repaglinide: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration with cyclosporine should be avoided. 32. Repotrectinib: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration with CYP3A inhibitors should be avoided. 33. Rifampin: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 34. Selumetinib: Letermovir increases its levels. If co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the selumetinib dose. 35. Siponimod: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration with moderate or strong CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 inhibitors is not recommended. 36. Sotorasib: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 37. St. John’s Wort: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 38. Tazemetostat: Letermovir increases its levels. Co-administration with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. 39. Tenofovir (AF and DF): These drugs decrease letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 40. Tepotinib: Letermovir increases its levels. If unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage. 41. Tipranavir: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 42. Trofinetide: Letermovir levels may increase due to OATP1B1/1B3 inhibition. Co-administration should be avoided. 43. Vinblastine: This drug decreases letermovir levels via P-gp induction. Co-administration is not recommended. 44. Acarbose: Letermovir increases its levels. Monitor glucose concentrations closely. 45. Alfentanil: Letermovir increases its levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 46. Alfuzosin: Letermovir increases its levels. Use caution and monitor closely. 47. Aliskiren: Letermovir increases its levels. Use caution and monitor closely. In summary, letermovir has significant drug-drug interactions primarily mediated by CYP3A4 and P-gp pathways. Careful consideration of co-administered medications is essential to avoid adverse effects or reduced efficacy.
